forces.title: Global electronics supply chains shift from cost to resilience
forces.description: The traditional logic of global electronics supply chains, focused solely on optimizing unit cost and concentrating manufacturing, is undergoing structural transformation. Driven by geopolitical risk re-pricing, the need for supply chain resilience after COVID-19, and regulatory pressures (e.g., U.S. CHIPS Act, India's PLI), OEMs are pivoting to multi-node manufacturing networks. This elevates EMS providers to strategic supply chain partners.

forces.title: Megatrends boost global EMS industry demand
forces.description: The global EMS industry is experiencing significant expansion, driven by three key megatrends. The proliferation of connected devices like smartphones and IoT systems, the increasing electrification and automation across industries (automotive, energy), and the growing trend of OEMs outsourcing manufacturing to manage complexity and reduce capital investment are fueling strong demand for electronics manufacturing capacity worldwide.

forces.title: Thin depth in quality certifications restricts high-value EMS market access
forces.description: India's EMS industry has thin depth across critical quality certifications such as IATF 16949 (automotive), AS9100D (aerospace/defense), and ISO 13485 (medical devices). Achieving these certifications requires significant, sustained investment and years of effort, acting as a competitive moat for incumbents. This lack of certification depth limits India's access to higher-value, regulated segments of the EMS market, despite its scaling capacity.

forces.title: High FDI inflows boost India's computer software and hardware sector
forces.description: India's computer software and hardware sector has attracted substantial foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows, totaling US$ 110.16 billion between April 2000 and June 2025. This significant capital inflow, ranking the sector second in cumulative FDI equity inflows, reflects strong investor confidence and provides a crucial tailwind for the growth and expansion of technology hardware and equipment manufacturing and development in the country.

forces.title: Regulatory incentives drive electronics manufacturing geographic diversification
forces.description: Regulatory pressures, including the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act 2022, the EU Chips Act 2023, and India's production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes, are creating significant fiscal incentives for geographic diversification of electronics manufacturing. These policies reinforce the commercial logic for OEMs to build more resilient and diversified production networks, positioning India as a key beneficiary of this global shift.

forces.title: India's EMS faces domestic component supply chain absence
forces.description: India's most structurally significant vulnerability in its rapidly growing EMS industry is the absence of a deep, domestic component supply chain. This leads to high reliance on long-haul import supply chains for critical components like semiconductors, displays, and PCBs. Consequently, domestically assembled products carry high embedded import content, constraining value capture and margin retention within India's EMS sector.

forces.title: 5G and IoT drive accelerated electronics product adoption
forces.description: Technology transitions such as the widespread rollout of 5G networks and the increasing adoption of the Internet of Things (IoT) are driving accelerated adoption of electronics products. These advancements create significant demand for new and upgraded hardware, including communications and networking equipment, embedded systems, and various electronic components, acting as a strong tailwind for the Technology Hardware & Equipment sector.

forces.title: Talent pyramid reinvention crucial for AI-first world
forces.description: To achieve ownership in the next phase of technology growth, India must reinvent its tech talent pyramid by reskilling at scale for an AI-first world. This involves national skilling coalitions, deeper academia-industry integration, and deliberate inclusion. This structural change is essential to meet the evolving demands of capital-intensive, IP-led, and R&D-driven hardware segments like semiconductors and deep tech.

forces.title: Shift towards design-integrated EMS for higher value creation
forces.description: The EMS industry is evolving beyond high-volume, thin-margin assembly toward design-integrated manufacturing. Leading global EMS players are expanding their capabilities to include design support, engineering services, and product development, enabling them to capture significantly higher margins and strategic positioning. This structural shift requires organizational capability and engineering depth rather than just capital investment.

forces.title: Productivity gaps limit India's EMS competitiveness in precision manufacturing
forces.description: Despite India's large labor pool, it faces productivity gaps in EMS operations compared to established hubs like China and Vietnam. These gaps are driven by lower automation density, limited exposure to complex manufacturing programs, and uneven availability of skilled technicians. This partially offsets India’s labor cost advantage, hindering its ability to compete in high-precision and high-reliability applications, especially where quality and yield are paramount.

forces.title: Defense, data centers, infrastructure drive new industrial-tech demand
forces.description: New value pools are emerging for industrial technology suppliers, with defense buildups, data centers, and infrastructure renewal projected to account for $1.1 trillion in additional demand by 2030. These sectors create significant opportunities for hardware in areas such as AI-driven control systems, sensors, precision robotics, specialized machinery, and complex components, offering long-term, high-margin contracts for suppliers.

forces.title: Government policies and incentives accelerate ESDM growth
forces.description: Government initiatives such as the Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes for large-scale electronics and IT hardware, the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) 2.0, and the Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS) are providing robust policy support. These schemes attract significant investments, boost production, and strengthen domestic supply chains for chips and components, acting as powerful tailwinds for the ESDM sector.

forces.title: Micron's ATMP facility boosts India's semiconductor ecosystem
forces.description: Micron Technology's inauguration of India’s first semiconductor ATMP (Assembly, Testing, Marking, and Packaging) facility, backed by a US$ 2.75 billion investment, is a significant tailwind. This facility is crucial for advancing assembly, testing, and R&D for AI-enabling chips, contributing substantially to India's semiconductor ecosystem and driving demand for related manufacturing equipment and processes within the Technology Hardware & Equipment sector.

forces.title: India becomes major mobile phone production and export hub
forces.description: India has become the world’s second-largest mobile phone manufacturer, with production reaching US$ 61.6 billion in 2024–25 and exports surging to US$ 22.56 billion. The country also overtook China as the top smartphone exporter to the US in Q2 FY26. This strong growth in production and exports, coupled with increasing domestic demand and premium segment growth, represents a significant tailwind for consumer electronics and devices.

forces.title: India's limited presence in high-growth hardware segments
forces.description: India's technology market is largely concentrated in IT services, with limited presence in high-growth, capital-intensive, IP-led, and R&D-driven segments such as Hyperscale cloud platforms, Semiconductors, Deep Tech, and AI-native offerings. This poses a key risk as these segments are expected to drive disproportionate value creation in the coming decade, requiring India to make strategic 'big bets' to address this gap.

viewpoints.title: India's EMS sector benefits from global supply chain realignment
viewpoints.description: KPMG highlights that global OEMs are restructuring supply chains around resilience, geopolitics, and multi-node manufacturing. Electronic Manufacturing Services (EMS) providers are central to this shift. India's opportunity in EMS is not merely cost-based but stems from geopolitical and strategic factors, positioning it as a potential alternative node in the global electronics supply chain.

viewpoints.title: India needs strategic shift towards high-growth hardware segments
viewpoints.description: India's current technology market strength is heavily concentrated in IT Consulting and Services. However, the next decade's disproportionate value creation is expected from capital-intensive, IP-led, and R&D-driven segments such as Hyperscale cloud platforms, Semiconductors, Deep Tech, and AI-native offerings. India needs to make strategic, high-conviction investments to build its presence in these hardware and component-intensive areas.

viewpoints.title: National Policy on Electronics targets India as global ESDM hub
viewpoints.description: The National Policy on Electronics (NPE) 2019 aims to position India as a global hub for Electronics System Design and Manufacturing (ESDM). This vision includes encouraging and driving capabilities for developing core components, including chipsets, and creating an enabling environment for the industry to compete globally. The government places high priority on electronics hardware manufacturing.

viewpoints.title: India transitioning to execution phase in technology and manufacturing
viewpoints.description: India is moving from building foundational infrastructure to accelerated execution in technology and manufacturing sectors. Global players' continued investment signals confidence in India's growth story. The shift demands expanding design and manufacturing capabilities beyond mere volume, focusing on sophistication, Industry 4.0 systems, and automation to achieve value-chain leadership.

viewpoints.title: India's data center capacity poised for significant growth
viewpoints.description: India's Data Center capacity, currently 1.2 GW, is projected to quadruple to 4 GW by 2030. This growth is driven by increasing digitization, India's cost competitiveness in building Data Centers, and the rising adoption of Artificial Intelligence. CareEdge Ratings sees immense growth potential despite India's current capacity being significantly lower than the global average per internet user.
